source_metadata.title: Cannabidiol in Anxiety and Sleep: A Large Case Series

extraction_metadata.scope_note: Only primary-study assertions generated by this case series were atomized. Background literature and bibliography entries were not converted into primary-study atoms.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to determine whether CBD was helpful for improving sleep and/or anxiety in a clinical population.
The study also examined CBD tolerability, safety concerns, and patient acceptance.
Investigators conducted a retrospective chart review of adult psychiatric outpatients treated with CBD for anxiety or sleep as an adjunct to treatment as usual.
Eligible patients had a clinician-diagnosed sleep or anxiety disorder, consented to CBD treatment, and completed at least 1 month of active CBD treatment with follow-up.

population.label: Eligible adult psychiatric outpatients
inclusion_criteria: Clinician diagnosis of a sleep or anxiety disorder
At least 1 month of active CBD treatment with follow-up

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients with sole or primary schizophrenia, posttraumatic stress disorder, or agitated depression were excluded, and patients with only one documented visit were also excluded.

population.label: Sampling frame
exclusion_criteria: Sole or primary posttraumatic stress disorder
Only one documented visit with no follow-up assessment

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients continued routine psychiatric care, and most continued their psychiatric medications while CBD was added.

Nearly all patients received CBD 25 mg/day in capsule form; dosing was generally in the morning for predominant anxiety and in the evening for predominant sleep complaints, with a few patients receiving 50 or 75 mg/day and one patient titrated to 175 mg/day.

exposures.details: Nearly all patients received 25 mg/day. A handful received 50 or 75 mg/day; one patient was titrated to 175 mg/day. Timing depended on the dominant complaint.

atoms.canonical_statement: The Western Institutional Review Board approved the retrospective chart review, and informed consent was obtained for each patient treated and considered for the study.
The study was conducted at Wholeness Center, an integrative mental health and psychiatry clinic in Fort Collins, Colorado.

The sampling frame included 103 consecutively CBD-treated adults; 82 had a documented anxiety or sleep disorder, and the final analytic sample included 72 patients after diagnosis and follow-up exclusions.
The final sample included 47 patients with primary anxiety concerns and 25 patients with primary poor-sleep concerns.

population.label: Final analytic sample: 47 anxiety and 25 poor sleep

atoms.canonical_statement: Anxiety was assessed monthly with the 14-item Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, which ranges from 0 to 56; scores under 17 indicate mild anxiety and scores above 25 indicate severe anxiety.

outcome.definition: 14-item anxiety measure, range 0 to 56; source states <17 indicates mild anxiety and >25 severe anxiety.

atoms.canonical_statement: Sleep was assessed monthly with the 19-item Pittsburg Sleep Quality Index, which ranges from 0 to 21; higher scores indicate more sleep-related concerns and a score of 5 or greater indicates a poor sleeper.

outcome.definition: 19-item self-report sleep measure, range 0 to 21; higher scores indicate more sleep-related concerns and >=5 indicates poor sleeper.

atoms.canonical_statement: Side effects and tolerability were assessed through spontaneous patient self-reports documented in case records.
Deidentified patient data were analyzed with descriptive statistics and plotted for visual analysis and interpretation of trends.
Patients in the anxiety group had a mean age of 34 years with a range of 18 to 70 years, and 28 of 47 were men.
Patients in the sleep-disorder group had a mean age of 36.5 years with a range of 18 to 72 years, and 16 of 25 were women.
All 72 patients completed baseline and first-month assessments; 41 patients remained on CBD and completed the second-month assessment, and 27 remained on CBD at the third-month assessment.
At the first monthly assessment, 57 of 72 patients (79.2%) experienced improvement in anxiety.

atoms.canonical_statement: Four patients declined CBD treatment because of religious or ethical concerns about its relation to cannabis.
The naturalistic, open-label design and absence of a comparison group limit interpretation of efficacy.
Concurrent psychiatric medications and other mental health services such as counseling limit causal attribution to CBD.
Cannabis-related notoriety and patient preference for natural treatment may increase placebo effects and other bias.
The clinical sample was younger than the clinic population, creating potential selection bias.
Clinical attrition was substantial, and the reasons for later loss to follow-up were largely unknown.
The authors concluded that CBD may hold benefit for anxiety-related disorders, while sleep improvements were not sustained and controlled clinical studies are needed.
The authors stated that randomized and controlled trials are needed before definitive clinical guidance can be provided.

CV Sciences Inc provided the cannabidiol products; the authors reported that the company had no role in data collection, data interpretation, report preparation, or the decision to submit, and no other financial support was provided.

Scott Shannon disclosed professional books on integrative mental health and compensated work as a principal investigator for an MDMA-assisted psychotherapy study; the other authors reported no conflicts of interest.
